profiles.meeting_scenario: The meeting takes place in a software engineering team maintaining QChecker, a static analysis tool for Qiskit programs, after a regression report from an internal CI job showed that the latest branch suddenly flags far fewer issues on Bugs4Q and also times out on one large benchmark project. The immediate context is that a recent refactor touched both the AST extraction layer and several bug-pattern matchers to support newer Qiskit syntax. The agenda is to diagnose why detection coverage dropped and why runtime increased, decide whether the problem is in parsing, pattern evaluation, or benchmark setup, and agree on the quickest corrective action before the next demo build. The expected outcome is a shared plan for reproducing the issue, identifying the likely root cause, and assigning a fix path that can be completed today.

members.name: Priya Natarajan
members.expertise: Python AST tooling, rule-based bug detectors, Qiskit language constructs
members.background: Priya built much of QChecker's AST extraction pipeline and recently added support for newer circuit-building idioms introduced in recent Qiskit examples.
members.private_state: She wants to show that the core extractor refactor is sound and suspects the apparent regression is mostly noise from benchmark drift or from how results are being aggregated; she is also worried that reverting the parser changes would delay upcoming compatibility work.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the tool 'covers Bugs4Q', they mean the detector still finds at least one instance of each benchmark bug category somewhere in the suite, not necessarily the same total count as before.

The 'large benchmark project' everyone refers to is the v2 transpiler-heavy case added to the nightly suite last week, because that is the only one she expects to stress AST traversal enough to timeout.
If they 'rerun the benchmark', the normal procedure is to use QChecker's cached intermediate AST JSON artifacts from the previous preprocessing step so detector behavior can be compared in isolation.
A 'fix' for today's build means restoring detector outputs on the supported Qiskit 0.45-style code paths without having to normalize every legacy alias or deprecated import form immediately.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.expertise: Benchmark automation, regression triage, build pipelines, performance instrumentation
members.background: Marcus owns the Bugs4Q CI pipeline and the regression dashboard that compares issue counts and run times across QChecker branches.
members.private_state: He wants a stable pipeline result that matches the dashboard trend line and suspects the refactor changed what files or constructs are being analyzed; he is concerned that a subtle parsing omission will ship as a silent false negative problem.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the tool 'covers Bugs4Q', they mean the branch should reproduce roughly the same total number of benchmark findings as the last green baseline, because the dashboard compares counts at that level.
The 'large benchmark project' refers to the legacy chemistry benchmark in the scheduled CI suite, because that is the one whose wall-clock time triggered the alert email he investigated.
If they 'rerun the benchmark', the standard troubleshooting method is a clean CI-style execution from source checkout with caches disabled, since cached artifacts can hide extraction bugs.
A 'fix' for today's build means the branch should restore the baseline dashboard numbers and complete the full scheduled suite without timeout, including legacy examples still present in Bugs4Q.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to restore Bugs4Q coverage
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'get coverage back on Bugs4Q' before the demo build.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means recovering semantic coverage across benchmark bug categories so the detector still demonstrates capability, even if the raw number of matched findings differs from the old baseline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus means restoring the branch to approximately the previous total finding count shown on the CI dashboard, since that is the operational definition of regression recovery in his pipeline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound like normal interpretations of 'coverage' in a troubleshooting context, and because they are trying to act quickly, neither thinks to unpack whether they mean category-level detection or count-level parity.

misalignment_points.topic: Which benchmark case is timing out
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention 'the large benchmark project' as the main runtime problem.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is thinking of the newer transpiler-heavy benchmark added to nightly runs, whose nested circuit-construction code she expects to stress recursive AST extraction.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus is thinking of the legacy chemistry benchmark from the scheduled CI suite, because that specific job emitted the timeout alert on his dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There are only a few well-known heavy benchmarks in their environment, so saying 'the large benchmark project' feels sufficiently specific to both; each assumes the other saw the same alert or test list.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'rerun the benchmark with logging' to isolate whether extraction or matching is at fault.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya plans to rerun detector logic against cached AST artifacts so she can compare pattern matcher outputs without the noise of preprocessing differences.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus plans a clean end-to-end CI-style rerun from raw source with caches disabled so any extraction regression will reappear.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using logging on a rerun sounds like a shared troubleshooting step, but each person's usual workflow bakes in a different execution method that they consider the obvious default and therefore leave unstated.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they only need a 'fix for today's build' rather than a full cleanup.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya assumes the fix can be narrowly scoped to modern supported Qiskit syntax paths and the detector behavior exercised in the demo environment.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Marcus assumes the fix must also restore the scheduled full-suite CI behavior, including legacy import styles and older benchmark examples still counted on the dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In release-pressure situations, 'today's build' usually implies a temporary practical fix, and both think they are being appropriately pragmatic; the hidden disagreement is over which code paths are implicitly in scope.

turns.inner_thought: The branch drop looks worse on paper than it probably is. If the refactor still lets us detect at least one instance of each Bugs4Q bug category, then we basically still cover Bugs4Q in the sense that matters for the demo. I really do not want this to turn into a parser rollback, because that would block the compatibility work for the newer Qiskit circuit-building patterns. For today's build, I just need the modern 0.45-style paths behaving again; we can defer all the old alias cleanup.
turns.utterance: I looked through the latest branch results, and we definitely dropped coverage on Bugs4Q after the AST refactor. Before the demo build, we need to get coverage back and land a fix for today's build, not turn this into a full cleanup.

turns.inner_thought: Coverage means the dashboard count needs to come back up near the last green baseline, otherwise the pipeline still reads as regressed. And the timeout is on the legacy chemistry benchmark from scheduled CI, not just some nightly oddity. If extraction changed what files or constructs get analyzed, that would explain both the finding count collapse and the wall-clock spike.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and CI also flagged a timeout on the large benchmark project, so I’m not convinced this is only one thing. It could be a mix of extraction changes and how the results are getting reported.

turns.inner_thought: The extractor refactor was targeted; I doubt it suddenly broke everything end-to-end. The fastest way to isolate it is to rerun the benchmark with logging against the cached AST JSON so I can compare detector behavior without preprocessing noise. If findings are already missing in the cached artifacts, that's a matcher issue; if not, then aggregation is muddying things.
turns.utterance: The parser-side changes were actually pretty contained, so I’d rather not assume the extractor is the whole problem yet. We should rerun the benchmark with logging and check whether the findings disappear before or after pattern matching.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I’ll do a clean CI-style rerun from source with caches off and enough logging to show exactly where the counts diverge. What matters most is whether the total findings come back to baseline, because that’s what the dashboard is comparing and that’s what release review will look at.
turns.utterance: Agreed. Let’s rerun the benchmark with logging, and I mainly want to see where the dashboard count starts diverging from the last green baseline.

turns.inner_thought: We should start with the new transpiler-heavy benchmark, since that’s the obvious stress case for the recursive traversal changes and the newer circuit-construction wrappers I added support for. If unresolved call nodes increased there, that would line up perfectly with the refactor.
turns.utterance: I’d start with the large benchmark project, because its newer circuit-building style is exactly the kind of thing where the node extraction behavior changed.

turns.inner_thought: The chemistry benchmark has always been the one that wobbles on runtime, so I’m not surprised it’s where we saw the alert. My priority is still the full scheduled suite: if that doesn’t finish cleanly today, we can’t call the build fixed no matter what the narrower checks say.
turns.utterance: That makes sense, although the large benchmark project has been flaky before. What I especially care about is that the full scheduled suite gets through cleanly today.

turns.inner_thought: If we still hit every benchmark bug category somewhere in the suite, then the detector capability is intact enough for now. In that case, today's fix should stay tightly scoped to the modern supported syntax paths instead of dragging in every legacy import alias and deprecated form that still exists in old benchmarks.
turns.utterance: Right, and if the bug categories are still being detected, then a fix for today’s build can stay pretty narrow while we clean up older syntax handling afterward.

turns.inner_thought: Narrow is fine only if the dashboard looks normal again. I need the total counts to line back up with the baseline trend and stop looking like a silent false-negative regression. If the numbers are still low, nobody in CI will consider this recovered.
turns.utterance: That sounds fine to me as long as coverage is back and the benchmark numbers line up again for the release dashboard.

turns.inner_thought: I want visibility into the extractor itself. On my rerun, using the cached AST artifacts, I can add counters for unresolved call nodes and compare them against matcher inputs. If the matcher is being starved because wrappers aren’t normalized the way I expect, that will show up quickly.
turns.utterance: I can also instrument the AST extractor to count unresolved call nodes and compare that against a rerun, which should tell us whether the matcher is being starved of input.

turns.inner_thought: I’ll launch the rerun directly from the CI job definition, clean checkout, caches disabled, with timing breakdowns so I can see whether extraction, matching, or postprocessing is burning time on the chemistry benchmark. That should reproduce whatever the scheduled pipeline saw.
turns.utterance: Great. I’ll kick off the rerun with logging from the CI job definition and attach timing breakdowns for the large benchmark project so we can see where the time is going.

turns.inner_thought: If the logs point to misses in the newer syntax wrappers, I can patch that traversal path today and avoid reopening the broader legacy normalization problem. That should be enough to restore the demo-relevant modern code paths without touching every old example style.
turns.utterance: If the logs show extraction misses only on newer syntax wrappers, I’ll patch that path first so the build is fixed today.

turns.inner_thought: Once her patch lands, I’ll compare the rerun against the last green dashboard baseline and make sure the total findings and runtime are back where they should be across the full suite. If the counts are still off, we’re not done, even if one path looks better.
turns.utterance: Perfect. Once your patch is in, I’ll compare the rerun against the baseline dashboard and we can confirm that coverage is restored.
